\section[deshacer]{deshacer — to undo; to unpack}

\label{lesson:ES-C668-deshacer}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the tenant, then the Spanish for to rent.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: deshacer}
\textbf{deshacer} — \textquotedblleft{}to undo; to unpack\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Deshago la maleta al llegar.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{I unpack my case when I arrive.}
\end{quote}

Conjugated like \emph{hacer}: \emph{deshago}, \emph{deshice}. \emph{Deshacer la maleta} — to unpack.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{deshacer} is built on \emph{hacer} \textquotedblleft{}to make, to do\textquotedblright{} with \emph{des-} "un-"; \emph{hacer} is inherited from Latin \emph{facere}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{deshacer}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{deshacer}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{deshacer}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for the tenant, then the Spanish for to rent, then say \emph{deshacer} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does deshacer mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To undo; to unpack\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.

\section[empaquetar]{empaquetar — to pack up, to wrap up}

\label{lesson:ES-C668-empaquetar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to rent, then the Spanish for to undo.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: empaquetar}
\textbf{empaquetar} — \textquotedblleft{}to pack up, to wrap up\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Empaqueto los regalos antes del viaje.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{I wrap up the presents before the trip.}
\end{quote}

Built on \emph{el paquete}, the parcel.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{empaquetar} is built on \emph{paquete} \textquotedblleft{}parcel\textquotedblright{}, which came from French \emph{paquet} (EtymDB), from Dutch \emph{pak} \textquotedblleft{}bundle\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[la báscula]{la báscula — the scales (for weighing)}

\label{lesson:ES-C668-bascula}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to undo, then the Spanish for to pack up.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la báscula}
\textbf{la báscula} — \textquotedblleft{}the scales (for weighing)\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Pon la maleta en la báscula.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Put the suitcase on the scales.}
\end{quote}

In the bathroom it weighs you; at the airport it weighs your bag.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{báscula} comes from French \emph{bascule} \textquotedblleft{}seesaw\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB): old scales tipped like a seesaw.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[el exceso]{el exceso — the excess}

\label{lesson:ES-C668-exceso}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to pack up, then the Spanish for the scales.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el exceso}
\textbf{el exceso} — \textquotedblleft{}the excess\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Pagué cincuenta euros por exceso de equipaje.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{I paid fifty euros for excess baggage.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Exceso de equipaje} — excess baggage.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{exceso} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{excessus} \textquotedblleft{}a going out, a departure\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short), from \emph{excēdere} \textquotedblleft{}to go beyond\textquotedblright{}, built on \emph{cēdere} \textquotedblleft{}to go\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[arrastrar]{arrastrar — to drag, to pull along}

\label{lesson:ES-C668-arrastrar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the scales, then the Spanish for the excess.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: arrastrar}
\textbf{arrastrar} — \textquotedblleft{}to drag, to pull along\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Arrastro la maleta por la calle.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{I drag my suitcase along the street.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Arrastrar los pies} — to shuffle your feet.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{arrastrar} is built from \emph{a-} and \emph{rastrar}, on \emph{rastro} \textquotedblleft{}trail\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), which comes from Latin \emph{rāstrum} \textquotedblleft{}a rake\textquotedblright{}, from \emph{rādere} \textquotedblleft{}to scrape\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}
